text: Quantum computing occupies an unusual position among emerging technologies: it is simultaneously the subject of formidable scientific achievement and of hype so pervasive that separating genuine progress from speculative marketing has become its own discipline. The underlying physics is not in dispute—superposition and entanglement allow a qubit to encode vastly more information than a classical bit, and certain algorithms could, in principle, solve problems currently considered computationally intractable in exponentially less time. Proponents argue this represents a genuine paradigm shift, one capable of rendering conventional encryption obsolete within a decade. Skeptics counter that today's quantum processors remain rudimentary, plagued by decoherence, and that no one has yet demonstrated a scalable, fault-tolerant system capable of outperforming classical computers on a practically useful problem. Both camps have a point: the theoretical case for quantum advantage is formidable, but the engineering path to a commercially viable machine remains genuinely uncertain, and viability at laboratory scale is a poor predictor of viability at industrial scale. What is disruptive in principle is not necessarily disruptive in practice, at least not yet. Investors would do well to remember that every transformative technology has, at some stage, been both overhyped and underestimated simultaneously.
